verdict.claim: The authors study structural equivalences and conjectures for the circuit diameter, a relaxation/variant of the combinatorial diameter where walks follow circuit directions rather than edges of the 1-skeleton.
verdict.evidence: We consider analogous properties for a variant of the combinatorial diameter called the circuit diameter.
verdict.caveat: The results pertain to circuit diameter rather than the standard combinatorial diameter of polytopes.

signals.title: Circuit Diameter of Polyhedra is Strongly Polynomial
signals.abstract: We prove a strongly polynomial bound on the circuit diameter of polyhedra, resolving the circuit analogue of the polynomial Hirsch conjecture. Specifically, we show that the circuit diameter of a polyhedron $P = \{x\in \mathbb{R}^n:\, A x = b, \, x \ge 0\}$ with $A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}$ is $O(m^2 \log m)$. Our construction yields monotone circuit walks, giving the same bound for the monotone circuit diameter. The circuit diameter, introduced by Borgwardt, Finhold, and Hemmecke (SIDMA 2015), is a natural relaxation of the combinatorial diameter that allows steps along circuit directions rather than only along edges. All prior upper bounds on the circuit diameter were only weakly polynomial. Finding a circuit augmentation algorithm that matches this bound would yield a strongly polynomial time algorithm for linear programming, resolving Smale's 9th problem.

verdict.claim: The authors establish a strongly polynomial upper bound on the circuit diameter of polyhedra, which is a relaxation of the combinatorial diameter.
verdict.evidence: We prove a strongly polynomial bound on the circuit diameter of polyhedra, resolving the circuit analogue of the polynomial Hirsch conjecture.
verdict.caveat: The result bounds the circuit diameter rather than the combinatorial diameter; because circuit steps relax edge steps, an upper bound on circuit diameter does not imply a polynomial upper bound on the combinatorial diameter.

problems.title: The sunflower conjecture
problems.statement: Erdős–Rado: is there a constant $C$ such that any family of more than $C^k$ sets of size $k$ contains three sets forming a sunflower (pairwise intersections all equal to a common core)?
problems.why: Sunflower-free families are the combinatorial obstruction behind several circuit lower bound techniques and matrix multiplication approaches, so the bound's shape propagates directly into complexity theory.

evidence.text: Erdős–Rado's original bound is $k!\,C^k$; the conjecture is that the factorial can be removed.
Alweiss, Lovett, Wu and Zhang brought it down to $(\log k)^{k(1+o(1))}$ via a spread-approximation / random restriction argument — the first improvement of the exponent's shape in sixty years.
Rao, and independently Bell–Chueluecha–Warnke, simplified and slightly improved the constant, but $C^k$ remains out of reach.

signals.title: Which NP-Hard SAT and CSP Problems Admit Exponentially Improved Algorithms?
signals.abstract: We study the complexity of SAT($Γ$) problems for potentially infinite languages $Γ$ closed under variable negation (sign-symmetric languages). Via an algebraic connection, this reduces to the study of restricted partial polymorphisms of $Γ$ we refer to as \emph{pSDI-operations} (for partial, self-dual and idempotent). First, we study the language classes themselves. We classify the structure of the least restrictive pSDI-operations, corresponding to the most powerful languages $Γ$, and find that these operations can be divided into \emph{levels}, corresponding to a rough notion of difficulty; and that within each level there is a strongest operation (the partial $k$-NU operation, preserving $(k-1)$-SAT) and a weakest operation (the $k$-universal operation $u_k$, preserving problems definable via bounded-degree polynomials). We show that every sign-symmetric $Γ$ not preserved by $u_k$ implements all $k$-clauses; thus if $Γ$ is not preserved by $u_k$ for any $k$, then SAT($Γ$) is trivially SETH-hard and cannot be solved faster than $O^*(2^n)$ unless SETH fails. Second, we study upper and lower bounds for SAT($Γ$) for such languages. We show that several classes in the hierarchy correspond to problems which can be solved faster than $2^n$ using previously known algorithmic strategies such as Subset Sum-style meet-in-the-middle and fast matrix multiplication. Furthermore, if the sunflower conjecture holds for sunflowers with k sets, then the partial k-NU language has an improved algorithm via local search. Complementing this, we show that for every class there is a concrete low

verdict.claim: The authors do not claim to advance or resolve the sunflower conjecture itself, but rather use it as a conditional hypothesis to yield faster algorithms for certain SAT problems.
verdict.evidence: Furthermore, if the sunflower conjecture holds for sunflowers with k sets, then the partial k-NU language has an improved algorithm via local search.
verdict.caveat: The paper assumes the sunflower conjecture to prove algorithmic results rather than proving any new bounds on the conjecture itself.

signals.title: A Structural Theorem for Local Algorithms with Applications to Coding, Testing, and Verification
signals.abstract: We prove a general structural theorem for a wide family of local algorithms, which includes property testers, local decoders, and PCPs of proximity. Namely, we show that the structure of every algorithm that makes $q$ adaptive queries and satisfies a natural robustness condition admits a sample-based algorithm with $n^{1- 1/O(q^2 \log^2 q)}$ sample complexity, following the definition of Goldreich and Ron (TOCT 2016). We prove that this transformation is nearly optimal. Our theorem also admits a scheme for constructing privacy-preserving local algorithms. Using the unified view that our structural theorem provides, we obtain results regarding various types of local algorithms, including the following. - We strengthen the state-of-the-art lower bound for relaxed locally decodable codes, obtaining an exponential improvement on the dependency in query complexity; this resolves an open problem raised by Gur and Lachish (SICOMP 2021). - We show that any (constant-query) testable property admits a sample-based tester with sublinear sample complexity; this resolves a problem left open in a work of Fischer, Lachish, and Vasudev (FOCS 2015) by extending their main result to adaptive testers. - We prove that the known separation between proofs of proximity and testers is essentially maximal; this resolves a problem left open by Gur and Rothblum (ECCC 2013, Computational Complexity 2018) regarding sublinear-time delegation of computation. Our techniques strongly rely on relaxed sunflower lemmas and the Hajnal-Szemerédi theorem.

verdict.claim: The authors do not claim to advance the sunflower conjecture itself, but rather utilize relaxed sunflower lemmas as a technique to prove structural theorems for local algorithms.
verdict.evidence: Our techniques strongly rely on relaxed sunflower lemmas and the Hajnal-Szemerédi theorem.
verdict.caveat: The paper applies existing or variant sunflower lemmas as a tool to tackle problems in property testing and coding theory, rather than attempting to prove new bounds for the Erdős–Rado sunflower conjecture.

signals.title: On the Second Kahn--Kalai Conjecture
signals.abstract: For any given graph $H$, we are interested in $p_\mathrm{crit}(H)$, the minimal $p$ such that the Erdős-Rényi graph $G(n,p)$ contains a copy of $H$ with probability at least $1/2$. Kahn and Kalai (2007) conjectured that $p_\mathrm{crit}(H)$ is given up to a logarithmic factor by a simpler "subgraph expectation threshold" $p_\mathrm{E}(H)$, which is the minimal $p$ such that for every subgraph $H'\subseteq H$, the Erdős-Rényi graph $G(n,p)$ contains \emph{in expectation} at least $1/2$ copies of $H'$. It is trivial that $p_\mathrm{E}(H) \le p_\mathrm{crit}(H)$, and the so-called "second Kahn-Kalai conjecture" states that $p_\mathrm{crit}(H) \lesssim p_\mathrm{E}(H) \log e(H)$ where $e(H)$ is the number of edges in $H$. In this article, we present a natural modification $p_\mathrm{E, new}(H)$ of the Kahn--Kalai subgraph expectation threshold, which we show is sandwiched between $p_\mathrm{E}(H)$ and $p_\mathrm{crit}(H)$. The new definition $p_\mathrm{E, new}(H)$ is based on the simple observation that if $G(n,p)$ contains a copy of $H$ and $H$ contains \emph{many} copies of $H'$, then $G(n,p)$ must also contain \emph{many} copies of $H'$. We then show that $p_\mathrm{crit}(H) \lesssim p_\mathrm{E, new}(H) \log e(H)$, thus proving a modification of the second Kahn--Kalai conjecture. The bound follows by a direct application of the set-theoretic "spread" property, which led to recent breakthroughs in the sunflower conjecture by Alweiss, Lovett, Wu and Zhang and the first fractional Kahn--Kalai conjecture by Frankston, Kahn, Narayanan and Park.

verdict.claim: The authors do not claim any progress on the sunflower conjecture itself, but instead apply the set-theoretic spread property developed in recent sunflower breakthroughs to a variant of the second Kahn--Kalai conjecture.
verdict.evidence: The bound follows by a direct application of the set-theoretic "spread" property, which led to recent breakthroughs in the sunflower conjecture by Alweiss, Lovett, Wu and Zhang and the first fractional Kahn--Kalai conjecture by Frankston, Kahn, Narayanan and Park.
verdict.caveat: Nothing obvious from the abstract

problems.title: The union-closed sets conjecture
problems.statement: Frankl: in every finite union-closed family of sets other than $\{\emptyset\}$, is there an element contained in at least half the sets?
problems.why: Elementary to state, resistant for forty years, and in 2022 it fell to an information-theoretic argument nobody had tried — which is why the remaining gap between $0.38$ and $0.5$ is now watched closely.

evidence.text: Gilmer broke the problem open with an entropy argument giving a constant of about $0.01$, the first constant bound of any kind.
Several groups independently pushed Gilmer's method to $(3-\sqrt5)/2\approx0.3819$, which is the natural barrier of that argument.
Getting from $0.3819$ to $1/2$ appears to need a genuinely different idea; the entropy method's own analysis caps out there.

signals.title: On supratopologies, normalized families and Frankl conjecture
signals.abstract: We introduce some generalized topological concepts to deal with union-closed families, and show that one can reduce the proof of Frankl's conjecture to some families of so-called supratopological spaces. We prove some results on the structure of normalized families, presenting a new way of reducing such a family to a smaller one using dual families. Applying our reduction method, we prove a refinement of a conjecture originally proposed by Poonen. Finally, we show that Frankl's Conjecture holds for the class of families obtained from successively applying the reduction process to a power set.

verdict.claim: The authors introduce structural reduction techniques for union-closed families and prove Frankl's conjecture for a specific subclass of families constructed from power sets via these reductions.
verdict.evidence: Finally, we show that Frankl's Conjecture holds for the class of families obtained from successively applying the reduction process to a power set.
verdict.caveat: The proof of Frankl's conjecture is restricted to a specific family generated by the authors' reduction process rather than the general conjecture.

signals.title: The Linear Relaxation of an Integer Program for the Union-Closed Conjecture
signals.abstract: The Frankl conjecture, also known as the union-closed sets conjecture, states that in any finite non-empty union-closed family, there exists an element in at least half of the sets. Let $f(n,a)$ be the maximum number of sets in a union-closed family on a ground set of $n$ elements where each element is in at most $a$ sets for some $a,n\in \mathbb{N}^+$. Proving that $f(n,a)\leq 2a$ for all $a, n \in \mathbb{N}^+$ is equivalent to proving the Frankl conjecture. By considering the linear relaxation of the integer programming formulation that was proposed in New Conjectures for Union-Closed Families by Pulaj, Raymond and Theis, we prove that $O(a^2)$ is an upper bound for $f(n,a)$. We also provide different ways that this result could be strengthened. Additionally, we give a new proof that $f(n,2^{n-1}-1)=2^n-n$.

verdict.claim: The authors study a linear relaxation of an integer programming formulation of Frankl's conjecture and prove an upper bound of $f(n,a) = O(a^2)$, whereas establishing $f(n,a) \le 2a$ would prove the conjecture.
verdict.evidence: By considering the linear relaxation of the integer programming formulation that was proposed in New Conjectures for Union-Closed Families by Pulaj, Raymond and Theis, we prove that $O(a^2)$ is an upper bound for $f(n,a)$.
verdict.caveat: The bound $f(n,a) = O(a^2)$ derived from the linear programming relaxation is substantially weaker than the $f(n,a) \le 2a$ bound required to resolve the union-closed sets conjecture.

problems.title: Hadwiger's conjecture on graph colouring
problems.statement: Is every graph with no $K_t$ minor $(t-1)$-colourable?
problems.why: It is the deepest generalisation of the four colour theorem — the case $t=5$ is equivalent to it, and $t=6$ was proved from it — so anything beyond $t=6$ would be a genuinely new colouring technique.

evidence.text: Robertson–Seymour–Thomas proved the case $t=6$, assuming the four colour theorem. Nothing beyond $t=6$ is known.
The best general bound gives $O(t\log\log t)$ colours (Delcourt–Postle), improving a long-standing $O(t\sqrt{\log t})$.

signals.title: Clique minors in graphs with a forbidden subgraph
signals.abstract: The classical Hadwiger conjecture dating back to 1940's states that any graph of chromatic number at least $r$ has the clique of order $r$ as a minor. Hadwiger's conjecture is an example of a well studied class of problems asking how large a clique minor one can guarantee in a graph with certain restrictions. One problem of this type asks what is the largest size of a clique minor in a graph on $n$ vertices of independence number $α(G)$ at most $r$. If true Hadwiger's conjecture would imply the existence of a clique minor of order $n/α(G)$. Results of Kuhn and Osthus and Krivelevich and Sudakov imply that if one assumes in addition that $G$ is $H$-free for some bipartite graph $H$ then one can find a polynomially larger clique minor. This has recently been extended to triangle free graphs by Dvořák and Yepremyan, answering a question of Norin. We complete the picture and show that the same is true for arbitrary graph $H$, answering a question of Dvořák and Yepremyan. In particular, we show that any $K_s$-free graph has a clique minor of order $c_s(n/α(G))^{1+\frac{1}{10(s-2) }}$, for some constant $c_s$ depending only on $s$. The exponent in this result is tight up to a constant factor in front of the $\frac{1}{s-2}$ term.

verdict.claim: The authors prove a lower bound on the size of a clique minor in $K_s$-free graphs as a function of independence number $\alpha(G)$ and vertex count $n$, addressing a variant problem inspired by Hadwiger's conjecture.
verdict.evidence: In particular, we show that any $K_s$-free graph has a clique minor of order $c_s(n/\alpha(G))^{1+\frac{1}{10(s-2)}}$, for some constant $c_s$ depending only on $s$.
verdict.caveat: The result applies to a restricted problem concerning $H$-free graphs and independence number rather than directly resolving or making major progress on Hadwiger's conjecture itself.

signals.title: Improved bound for improper colorings of graphs with no odd clique minor
signals.abstract: Strengthening Hadwiger's conjecture, Gerards and Seymour conjectured in 1995 that every graph with no odd $K_t$-minor is properly $(t-1)$-colorable, this is known as the Odd Hadwiger's conjecture. We prove a relaxation of the above conjecture, namely we show that every graph with no odd $K_t$-minor admits a vertex $(2t-2)$-coloring such that all monochromatic components have size at most $\lceil \frac{1}{2}(t-2) \rceil$. The bound on the number of colors is optimal up to a factor of $2$, improves previous bounds for the same problem by Kawarabayashi (2008), Kang and Oum (2019), Liu and Wood (2021), and strengthens a result by van den Heuvel and Wood (2018), who showed that the above conclusion holds under the more restrictive assumption that the graph is $K_t$-minor free. In addition, the bound on the component-size in our result is much smaller than those of previous results, in which the dependency on $t$ was non-explicit. Our short proof combines the method by van den Heuvel and Wood for $K_t$-minor free graphs with some additional ideas, which make the extension to odd $K_t$-minor free graphs possible.

verdict.claim: The author proves a relaxation of Hadwiger's conjecture showing that every graph with no odd $K_t$-minor admits a vertex $(2t-2)$-coloring with monochromatic components of size at most $\lceil \frac{1}{2}(t-2) \rceil$.
verdict.evidence: We prove a relaxation of the above conjecture, namely we show that every graph with no odd $K_t$-minor admits a vertex $(2t-2)$-coloring such that all monochromatic components have size at most $\lceil \frac{1}{2}(t-2) \rceil$.
verdict.caveat: The result establishes an improper (clustered) coloring with bounded monochromatic component sizes rather than the proper graph coloring required by Hadwiger's conjecture.

signals.title: The structure of quasi-transitive graphs avoiding a minor with applications to the domino problem
signals.abstract: An infinite graph is quasi-transitive if its vertex set has finitely many orbits under the action of its automorphism group. In this paper we obtain a structure theorem for locally finite quasi-transitive graphs avoiding a minor, which is reminiscent of the Robertson-Seymour Graph Minor Structure Theorem. We prove that every locally finite quasi-transitive graph $G$ avoiding a minor has a tree-decomposition whose torsos are finite or planar; moreover the tree-decomposition is canonical, i.e. invariant under the action of the automorphism group of $G$. As applications of this result, we prove the following. * Every locally finite quasi-transitive graph attains its Hadwiger number, that is, if such a graph contains arbitrarily large clique minors, then it contains an infinite clique minor. This extends a result of Thomassen (1992) who proved it in the 4-connected case and suggested that this assumption could be omitted. * Locally finite quasi-transitive graphs avoiding a minor are accessible (in the sense of Thomassen and Woess), which extends known results on planar graphs to any proper minor-closed family. * Minor-excluded finitely generated groups are accessible (in the group-theoretic sense) and finitely presented, which extends classical results on planar groups. * The domino problem is decidable in a minor-excluded finitely generated group if and only if the group is virtually free, which proves the minor-excluded case of a conjecture of Ballier and Stein (2018).
signals.comment: 46 pages, 4 figures. (Abstract shortened to meet arxiv requirements) v3: major revision
signals.journal_ref: Journal of Combinatorial Theory, Series B 169 (2024), 561-613

verdict.claim: The authors establish a Robertson-Seymour type structure theorem for locally finite quasi-transitive graphs avoiding a minor and show such graphs attain their Hadwiger number, but do not address the colouring aspect of Hadwiger's conjecture.
verdict.evidence: Every locally finite quasi-transitive graph attains its Hadwiger number, that is, if such a graph contains arbitrarily large clique minors, then it contains an infinite clique minor.
verdict.caveat: The paper focuses on structural graph theory for infinite graphs and decidability of the domino problem, without addressing graph colouring or bounds on the chromatic number.

problems.title: The Erdős–Hajnal conjecture
problems.statement: For every fixed graph $H$, is there $\epsilon(H)>0$ such that every $n$-vertex graph with no induced copy of $H$ contains a clique or independent set of size $n^{\epsilon}$?
problems.why: Random graphs only guarantee $\Theta(\log n)$; the conjecture says that forbidding any fixed induced subgraph forces polynomial structure. It has become the organising question of induced subgraph theory.

evidence.text: The general bound remains $e^{\Omega(\sqrt{\log n})}$ (Erdős–Hajnal's own), quasi-polynomial rather than polynomial.
The conjecture is proved for several families — all graphs on at most four vertices, the five-cycle $C_5$ (Chudnovsky, Scott, Seymour, Spirkl), and anything built from those by substitution.

signals.title: Pure pairs. I. Trees and linear anticomplete pairs
signals.abstract: The Erdos-Hajnal Conjecture asserts that for every graph H there is a constant c > 0 such that every graph G that does not contain H as an induced subgraph has a clique or stable set of cardinality at least |G|^c. In this paper, we prove a conjecture of Liebenau and Pilipczuk, that for every forest H there exists c > 0, such that every graph G contains either an induced copy of H, or a vertex of degree at least c|G|, or two disjoint sets of at least c|G| vertices with no edges between them. It follows that for every forest H there is c > 0 so that if G contains neither H nor its complement as an induced subgraph then there is a clique or stable set of cardinality at least |G|^c.

verdict.claim: , the authors prove that for every forest $H$, any graph $G$ excluding both $H$ and its complement $\overline{H}$ as induced subgraphs contains a clique or stable set of size at least $|G|^c$ for some constant $c > 0$.
verdict.evidence: It follows that for every forest H there is c > 0 so that if G contains neither H nor its complement as an induced subgraph then there is a clique or stable set of cardinality at least |G|^c.
verdict.caveat: The result is restricted to forests $H$ (and requires excluding both $H$ and its complement $\overline{H}$), rather than establishing the Erdős–Hajnal conjecture for all fixed graphs $H$.

signals.title: Polynomial bounds for chromatic number. IV. A near-polynomial bound for excluding the five-vertex path
signals.abstract: A graph G is H-free if it has no induced subgraph isomorphic to H. We prove that a $P_5$-free graph with clique number $ω\ge 3$ has chromatic number at most $ω^{\log_2(ω)}$. The best previous result was an exponential upper bound $(5/27)3^ω$, due to Esperet, Lemoine, Maffray, and Morel. A polynomial bound would imply that the celebrated Erdos-Hajnal conjecture holds for $P_5$, which is the smallest open case. Thus there is great interest in whether there is a polynomial bound for $P_5$-free graphs, and our result is an attempt to approach that.

verdict.claim: The authors establish a near-polynomial upper bound of $\omega^{\log_2(\omega)}$ on the chromatic number of $P_5$-free graphs, substantially improving upon the previous exponential bound toward settling the smallest open case of the Erdős–Hajnal conjecture.
verdict.evidence: We prove that a $P_5$-free graph with clique number $ω\ge 3$ has chromatic number at most $ω^{\log_2(ω)}$.
verdict.caveat: The result proves a near-polynomial bound rather than a polynomial bound, which means it approaches but does not fully resolve the Erdős–Hajnal conjecture even for the specific case of $P_5$.

signals.title: Excluding hooks and their complements
signals.abstract: The celebrated Erdos-Hajnal conjecture states that for every $n$-vertex undirected graph $H$ there exists $\eps(H)>0$ such that every graph $G$ that does not contain $H$ as an induced subgraph contains a clique or an independent set of size at least $n^{\eps(H)}$. A weaker version of the conjecture states that the polynomial-size clique/independent set phenomenon occurs if one excludes both $H$ and its complement $H^{\compl}$. We show that the weaker conjecture holds if $H$ is any path with a pendant edge at its third vertex; thus we give a new infinite family of graphs for which the conjecture holds.

verdict.claim: The authors prove a weaker variant of the Erdős–Hajnal conjecture—which requires excluding both $H$ and its complement $H^c$—for an infinite family of graphs $H$ defined as paths with a pendant edge at their third vertex.
verdict.evidence: We show that the weaker conjecture holds if $H$ is any path with a pendant edge at its third vertex; thus we give a new infinite family of graphs for which the conjecture holds.
verdict.caveat: The paper proves only a weaker variant of the Erdős–Hajnal conjecture (requiring exclusion of both $H$ and its complement $H^c$ rather than $H$ alone) for a specific family of graphs.

problems.title: The chromatic number of the plane
problems.statement: Hadwiger–Nelson: how many colours are needed to colour the plane so that no two points at distance exactly $1$ share a colour? It is known that $5\leq\chi\leq7$.
problems.why: Seventy-five years with a three-value gap, and the one move in that time came from a hand-built graph an amateur found — which keeps the problem unusually open to new constructions.

evidence.text: de Grey constructed a unit-distance graph with 1581 vertices and chromatic number 5, raising the lower bound from 4 for the first time since 1950.
The Polymath16 project reduced the smallest known 5-chromatic unit-distance graph to 509 vertices, without reaching 6.
The upper bound of 7 comes from a hexagonal tiling and has never been improved.

signals.title: A unit-distance graph in the plane with independence ratio below 1/4
signals.abstract: We prove that there exists a finite unit-distance graph in the plane with independence ratio strictly smaller than 1/4, answering a question of Erdős. Our proof closely follows the framework of Matolcsi, Ruzsa, Varga, and Zsámboki, based on the geometric fractional chromatic number, but adds a carefully chosen two-vertex augmentation that pushes their 27-vertex construction from geometric fractional chromatic number $4$ to a value strictly larger than 4. This disproves their Conjecture 1, and implies that the fractional chromatic number of the plane is strictly larger than 4. The proof can be made fully constructive, but the resulting finite graph has an enormous number of vertices.
signals.source: arXiv search: all:"chromatic number of the plane"

verdict.claim: The authors show that the fractional chromatic number of the plane is strictly greater than $4$, which concerns a related fractional variant of the problem but does not improve the known bounds $5 \le \chi \le 7$ on the ordinary chromatic number of the plane.
verdict.evidence: This disproves their Conjecture 1, and implies that the fractional chromatic number of the plane is strictly larger than 4.
verdict.caveat: The paper establishes a result on the fractional chromatic number and independence ratio, which does not improve the existing lower bound of $5$ for the chromatic number of the plane.

signals.title: The chromatic number of the plane with an interval of forbidden distances is at least 7
signals.abstract: The work is devoted to one of the variations of the Hadwiger--Nelson problem on the chromatic number of the plane. In this formulation one needs to find for arbitrarily small $\varepsilon$ the least possible number of colors needed to color a Euclidean plane in such a way that any two points, the distance between which belongs to the interval $[1-\varepsilon, 1+\varepsilon]$, are colored differently. The conjecture proposed by G. Exoo in 2004, states that for arbitrary positive $\varepsilon$ at least 7 colors are required. Also, with a sufficiently small $\varepsilon$ the number of colors is exactly 7. The main result of the present paper is that the conjecture is true for the Euclidean plane as well as for any Minkowski plane.
signals.comment: 16 pages, 6 figures. Extended the bibliography and details of proofs concerning arbitrary norm. Added a theorem on covering a disk of radius 3 by closed sets. Corrected some inaccuracies
signals.source: arXiv search: all:"chromatic number of the plane"

verdict.claim: The author proves that at least 7 colors are required to color the plane if the forbidden distance is expanded from $1$ to any interval $[1-\varepsilon, 1+\varepsilon]$ for $\varepsilon > 0$.
verdict.evidence: The main result of the present paper is that the conjecture is true for the Euclidean plane as well as for any Minkowski plane.
verdict.caveat: The result addresses a variation where an interval of distances $[1-\varepsilon, 1+\varepsilon]$ is forbidden, which yields a denser graph and does not improve the bounds for the single-distance Hadwiger--Nelson problem.

problems.title: The Erdős–Szekeres conjecture (happy ending problem)
problems.statement: Is $2^{n-2}+1$ the smallest number of points in general position in the plane that guarantees a convex $n$-gon?
problems.why: It is the founding problem of Ramsey theory in geometry, and the conjectured value has been matched by a construction since 1960 — only the upper bound resists.

evidence.text: Erdős–Szekeres gave a construction of $2^{n-2}$ points with no convex $n$-gon, which is conjectured to be extremal.
Suk proved an upper bound of $2^{n+o(n)}$, bringing the exponent's leading term to the conjectured value but not the lower-order terms.
Exact values are known only up to $n=6$, verified by computer search.

signals.title: On the Erdos-Szekeres convex polygon problem
signals.abstract: Let $ES(n)$ be the smallest integer such that any set of $ES(n)$ points in the plane in general position contains $n$ points in convex position. In their seminal 1935 paper, Erdos and Szekeres showed that $ES(n) \leq {2n - 4\choose n-2} + 1 = 4^{n -o(n)}$. In 1960, they showed that $ES(n) \geq 2^{n-2} + 1$ and conjectured this to be optimal. In this paper, we nearly settle the Erdos-Szekeres conjecture by showing that $ES(n) =2^{n +o(n)}$.

verdict.claim: The author claims an upper bound of $2^{n+o(n)}$ for the Erdős–Szekeres problem, matching the main term in the exponent of the conjectured $2^{n-2}+1$ bound.
verdict.evidence: In this paper, we nearly settle the Erdos-Szekeres conjecture by showing that $ES(n) =2^{n +o(n)}$.
verdict.caveat: The result determines the exponent's leading term but leaves lower-order terms open, so it does not establish the exact value $2^{n-2}+1$.

signals.title: On the representation of finite convex geometries with convex sets
signals.abstract: Very recently Richter and Rogers proved that any convex geometry can be represented by a family of convex polygons in the plane. We shall generalize their construction and obtain a wide variety of convex shapes for representing convex geometries. We present an Erdos-Szekeres type obstruction, which answers a question of Czedli negatively, that is general convex geometries cannot be represented with ellipses in the plane. Moreover, we shall prove that one cannot even bound the number of common supporting lines of the pairs of the representing convex sets. In higher dimensions we prove that all convex geometries can be represented with ellipsoids.

verdict.claim: The authors introduce an Erdős–Szekeres type obstruction for representing finite convex geometries using ellipses, but do not address the Erdős–Szekeres conjecture itself.
verdict.evidence: We present an Erdos-Szekeres type obstruction, which answers a question of Czedli negatively, that is general convex geometries cannot be represented with ellipses in the plane.
verdict.caveat: The result concerns representation theory of finite convex geometries rather than point configurations in general position guaranteeing convex $n$-gons.

signals.title: Ramsey Theory, Integer Partitions and a New Proof of the Erdos-Szekeres Theorem
signals.abstract: Let H be a k-uniform hypergraph whose vertices are the integers 1,...,N. We say that H contains a monotone path of length n if there are x_1 < x_2 < ... < x_{n+k-1} so that H contains all n edges of the form {x_i,x_{i+1},...,x_{i+k-1}}. Let N_k(q,n) be the smallest integer N so that every q-coloring of the edges of the complete k-uniform hypergraph on N vertices contains a monochromatic monotone path of length n. While the study of N_k(q,n) for specific values of k and q goes back (implicitly) to the seminal 1935 paper of Erdos and Szekeres, the problem of bounding N_k(q,n) for arbitrary k and q was studied by Fox, Pach, Sudakov and Suk. Our main contribution here is a novel approach for bounding the Ramsey-type numbers N_k(q,n), based on establishing a surprisingly tight connection between them and the enumerative problem of counting high-dimensional integer partitions. Some of the concrete results we obtain using this approach are the following: 1. We show that for every fixed q we have N_3(q,n)=2^{Θ(n^{q-1})}, thus resolving an open problem raised by Fox et al. 2. We show that for every k >= 3, N_k(2,n)=2^{\cdot^{\cdot^{2^{(2-o(1))n}}}} where the height of the tower is k-2, thus resolving an open problem raised by Elias and Matousek. 3. We give a new pigeonhole proof of the Erdős-Szekeres Theorem on cups-vs-caps, similar to Seidenberg's proof of the Erdos-Szekeres Lemma on increasing/decreasing subsequences.

verdict.claim: The authors introduce a new pigeonhole proof of the Erdős–Szekeres cups-vs-caps theorem and establish bounds for related hypergraph Ramsey numbers, but do not claim to improve the bounds for the Erdős–Szekeres conjecture itself.
verdict.evidence: We give a new pigeonhole proof of the Erdős-Szekeres Theorem on cups-vs-caps, similar to Seidenberg's proof of the Erdos-Szekeres Lemma on increasing/decreasing subsequences.
verdict.caveat: The abstract focuses on hypergraph Ramsey numbers and alternative proofs of classical foundational results rather than proving new bounds for the exact number of points guaranteeing a convex $n$-gon.

problems.title: The Erdős unit distance problem
problems.statement: What is the maximum number of unit distances determined by $n$ points in the plane? Erdős conjectured $n^{1+O(1/\log\log n)}$; the best known upper bound is $O(n^{4/3})$.
problems.why: Its sibling — the distinct distances problem — fell in 2010 to polynomial-method techniques, and those same techniques have so far made no dent here, which sharpens the question of what is different about it.

evidence.text: Spencer, Szemerédi and Trotter proved the $O(n^{4/3})$ upper bound; it has not been improved in forty years.
The lower bound comes from a $\sqrt n\times\sqrt n$ grid and is $n^{1+c/\log\log n}$ — superlinear but barely.
Guth–Katz's polynomial method settled the companion distinct distances problem up to a logarithmic factor, but does not transfer to unit distances.

signals.title: The Minkowski grid has robustly many repeated distances
signals.abstract: We show that there exists a constant $δ> 0$ such that for any positive integer $n$ there exists a set of $n$ points $P \subset \mathbb{R}^2$ with the following property: for every subset $A \subseteq P$ of size $|A| \geq 2$, \[ \max_{λ>0} \#\{(a,b)\in A \times A: a\ne b,\ \lvert a-b\rvert=λ\} \gtrsim \frac{|A|^2}{n^{1-δ}}.\] Our result is a vertical amplification of a robust Ramanujan estimate recently established by Croot-Mao-Pohoata-Sheffer-Yip for arbitrary subsets of the ordinary square grid, and is inspired by recent constructions for the Erdős unit distance problem and the Elekes-Rónyai problem. Taking $A=P$, the inequality above gives a distance occurring $n^{1+δ}$ times in $P$; thereby a scaled copy of $P$ is a counterexample for the unit-distance conjecture. In addition, the same inequality shows that (1) all subsets of $P$ of size $\gtrsim n^{1-δ}$ must contain isosceles triangles, and (2) all subsets of $P$ of size $\gtrsim n^{1/2-δ}$ must contain repeated distances. These features give polynomially improved estimates for old problems of Erdős. The existence of a set satisfying property (1) confirms a conjecture of Erdős from 1980, whereas the existence of a set with property (2) answers a question of Conlon-Fox-Gasarch-Harris-Ulrich-Zbarsky in the negative.

verdict.claim: The authors claim to construct a point set in the plane with $n^{1+\delta}$ occurrences of a single distance for some constant $\delta > 0$, thereby disproving Erdős's unit distance conjecture.
verdict.evidence: Taking $A=P$, the inequality above gives a distance occurring $n^{1+δ}$ times in $P$; thereby a scaled copy of $P$ is a counterexample for the unit-distance conjecture.
verdict.caveat: The preprint has not yet undergone peer review to verify the validity of its construction and proof.

signals.title: Furthest Pair Requires Quadratic Time in Superconstant Dimension under SETH
signals.abstract: Several fundamental problems in computational geometry admit algorithms with running time $f(d) \cdot n^{2-Θ(1/d)}$ for $n$ points in $d$ dimensions, making them among the most prominent examples of barely subquadratic computation. Notable members of this class include Furthest Pair, Bichromatic Closest Pair, (Bichromatic) Maximum Innter Product, and Hopcroft's Problem. Chen [Theory Comput. 2020] proved that, assuming the Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis (SETH), these problems require $n^{2-o(1)}$ time when the dimension satisfies $d=2^{Θ(\log^* n)}$. We extend this lower bound to all efficiently constructible dimensions $d=ω(1)$. Thus, assuming SETH, the dependence of the best known algorithms on the dimension is essentially unavoidable. The proof utilizes techniques in OpenAI's recent disproof of the Erdos unit distance conjecture. The proof was initially discovered by ChatGPT 5.5 Pro. The authors have validated and substantially edited the proof to improve the presentation.

verdict.claim: The authors do not claim a new bound on the Erdős unit distance problem, but instead prove fine-grained complexity lower bounds for the Furthest Pair problem under SETH.
verdict.evidence: The proof utilizes techniques in OpenAI's recent disproof of the Erdos unit distance conjecture.
verdict.caveat: The paper addresses computational complexity lower bounds for geometric algorithms under SETH rather than bounds on the maximum number of unit distances.

problems.title: Do EFX allocations always exist?
problems.statement: Given $n$ agents with additive valuations over indivisible goods, does an allocation that is envy-free up to any good (EFX) always exist? It is known for $n\leq3$; $n=4$ is open.
problems.why: EFX is the strongest fairness notion that is not obviously impossible for indivisible goods, and the fact that we cannot settle four agents makes it the sharpest open question in fair division.

evidence.text: Chaudhury, Garg and Mehlhorn proved existence for three agents with additive valuations; the argument does not extend to four.
Existence is known if a small number of goods may be discarded (partial EFX allocations with bounded charity).
No counterexample is known either, for any number of agents — the question is genuinely undecided, not merely unproved.

signals.title: EFX Allocations Exist on Multi-Graphs
signals.abstract: We study the fair allocation of indivisible goods among agents, with a focus on limiting envy. A central fairness notion is envy-freeness up to any good (EFX), which requires that any envy toward another agent vanishes after the removal of any single good from the latter's bundle. The existence of EFX allocations is considered a major open problem in fair division. So far, it has only been established in limited settings. Christodoulou et al. [2023] proved the existence of EFX allocations for graphical valuations. In this setting, the agents correspond to the nodes of an underlying graph, and the goods correspond to the edges, and any good has positive value only for the endpoints of the corresponding edge. Their proof crucially relies on the restriction that the graph is simple, meaning that for any pair of agents, there is at most one good that has value to both. For multigraph valuations, where multiple goods may be valued by the same pair of agents, only partial results are known. Amanatidis et al. [2024] and Kaviani et al. [2025] obtained 2/3 and sqrt(2)/2 approximations of EFX, respectively; Kaviani et al. [2024] established existence under restricted additive valuations; and Afshinmehr et al. [2025a] proved existence under the assumption that the shortest cycle containing non-parallel edges has length at least 4. In this paper, we resolve this open problem by proving the existence of EFX allocations for multigraph instances under cancelable valuations, a strict superclass of additive valuation functions. Our proof is algorithmic and computes such allocations in polyn

verdict.claim: The authors claim to prove the existence of EFX allocations for an arbitrary number of agents under multigraph valuations, a special case where each good is valued by at most two agents.
verdict.evidence: In this paper, we resolve this open problem by proving the existence of EFX allocations for multigraph instances under cancelable valuations, a strict superclass of additive valuation functions.
verdict.caveat: The result is restricted to multigraph valuations, where each good has positive value for at most two agents, rather than general additive valuations.

signals.title: EFX for Additive Chores: Nonexistence, Pareto Incompatibility, and Bi-Valued Existence
signals.abstract: We consider the fair division problem of indivisible chores and resolve the long-standing open problem for the existence of EFX (envy-free up to any item) allocations with additive cost functions. We show that, even for tri-valued additive cost functions, for every $n\geq 4$, there exists an instance with $n$ agents where no EFX allocation exists. Our counterexample only uses three types of chores and two types of agents. The numbers of types for chores and agents are both tight: an EFX allocation is known to exist for one type of agents (i.e., with identical cost functions) or two types of chores. We then consider bi-valued instances. We show that, for every $n\geq 4$, there exists an instance with $n$ agents where every EFX allocation is not Pareto-optimal. This is also the first example showing the incompatibility of EFX and Pareto-optimality when the costs of items are positive: existing examples showing the incompatibility of EFX and Pareto-optimal exploit items with $0$ costs. Our result shows such an example exists even for bi-valued instances. The number of agents $n$ is also tight: for $n\leq 3$, it is known that EFX is compatible with Pareto-optimality. Finally, we also show that an EFX allocation is guaranteed to exist for $n=4$.

verdict.claim: The authors claim to resolve the existence of EFX allocations for indivisible chores by showing that EFX allocations do not always exist for $n \geq 4$ agents with additive cost functions.
verdict.evidence: We show that, even for tri-valued additive cost functions, for every $n\geq 4$, there exists an instance with $n$ agents where no EFX allocation exists.
verdict.caveat: The result is for indivisible chores (additive cost functions) rather than indivisible goods (additive utility functions), so it does not settle the open problem for goods.

signals.title: Non-Existence of EFX Chore Allocations for Monotone Cost Functions with Binary Marginals
signals.abstract: We study the existence of envy-free up to any item (EFX) allocations of indivisible chores when agents have monotone cost functions with binary marginals. For indivisible goods, the corresponding existence question is known to have an affirmative answer for general monotone functions with binary marginals. For chores, however, the existence of EFX allocation was previously known only for more restricted classes, while the general binary-marginal case remained unresolved. In this paper, we provide two counterexamples based on the same 18-agent, 53-chore word gadget, with one cost profile for binary XOS costs and another for binary supermodular costs. In both cases, a complete EFX allocation need not exist. Finally, we formalize and verify our main results in Lean 4.

verdict.claim: The authors prove that complete EFX allocations do not always exist for indivisible chores when agents have binary XOS or binary supermodular cost functions.
verdict.evidence: In this paper, we provide two counterexamples based on the same 18-agent, 53-chore word gadget, with one cost profile for binary XOS costs and another for binary supermodular costs.
verdict.caveat: The paper studies indivisible chores with non-additive cost functions, whereas the open problem asks about indivisible goods with additive valuation functions.

problems.title: Polynomial envy-free cake cutting
problems.statement: Is there an envy-free cake-cutting protocol for $n$ agents using a number of queries polynomial in $n$ in the Robertson–Webb model?
problems.why: A bounded protocol exists, but its query count is a tower of exponentials — one of the largest gaps between 'finite' and 'usable' anywhere in the field.

evidence.text: Aziz and Mackenzie gave the first bounded envy-free protocol for any $n$, using $n^{n^{n^{n^{n^n}}}}$ queries.
The best lower bound is $\Omega(n^2)$ queries (Procaccia, 2009), leaving a gap of many orders of magnitude in the exponent tower.

signals.title: Truth, Justice, and Secrecy: Cake Cutting Under Privacy Constraints
signals.abstract: Cake-cutting algorithms, which aim to fairly allocate a continuous resource based on individual agent preferences, have seen significant progress over the past two decades. Much of the research has concentrated on fairness, with comparatively less attention given to other important aspects. Chen et al. (2010) introduced an algorithm that, in addition to ensuring fairness, was strategyproof -- meaning agents had no incentive to misreport their valuations. However, even in the absence of strategic incentives to misreport, agents may still hesitate to reveal their true preferences due to privacy concerns (e.g., when allocating advertising time between firms, revealing preferences could inadvertently expose planned marketing strategies or product launch timelines). In this work, we extend the strategyproof algorithm of Chen et al. by introducing a privacy-preserving dimension. To the best of our knowledge, we present the first private cake-cutting protocol, and, in addition, this protocol is also envy-free and strategyproof. Our approach replaces the algorithm's centralized computation with a novel adaptation of cryptographic techniques, enabling privacy without compromising fairness or strategyproofness. Thus, our protocol encourages agents to report their true preferences not only because they are not incentivized to lie, but also because they are protected from having their preferences exposed.
signals.comment: This is the full version of our paper published in the Proceedings of AAAI 2026

verdict.claim: The authors claim to construct a private, envy-free, and strategyproof cake-cutting protocol using cryptographic techniques, without addressing query complexity bounds in the Robertson–Webb model.
verdict.evidence: To the best of our knowledge, we present the first private cake-cutting protocol, and, in addition, this protocol is also envy-free and strategyproof.
verdict.caveat: The work focuses on privacy constraints and cryptographic multi-party computation rather than query complexity bounds for general valuation functions in the Robertson–Webb model.

problems.title: Approximating Nash equilibria in bimatrix games
problems.statement: What is the best constant $\epsilon$ for which an $\epsilon$-approximate Nash equilibrium of a two-player game can be found in polynomial time? The best known is slightly above $1/3$.
problems.why: Exact computation is PPAD-complete and a PTAS is ruled out under the exponential-time hypothesis for PPAD, so the whole question is where between $1/3$ and $0$ the true constant sits.

evidence.text: Tsaknakis–Spirakis gave a polynomial algorithm achieving $0.3393$, which stood as the best for fifteen years.
The constant was brought down to essentially $1/3$ (Deligkas, Fasoulakis, Markakis), the first improvement in fifteen years — and still a constant, not an approaching-zero sequence.
Rubinstein showed that under the ETH for PPAD there is no quasi-polynomial-time PTAS, so a constant barrier of some size is expected.

signals.title: The Complexity of Computing Coarse Correlated Equilibria in Markov Games with a Single Controller
signals.abstract: We study the complexity of computing stationary Markov coarse correlated equilibria (CCE) in discounted single-controller stochastic (Markov) games [PR81, FV97], a fundamental subclass of stochastic games in which all players may affect rewards, but only one player controls the state transitions. Prior work [DGZ23, JMS23, HN25] established PPAD-hardness for computing stationary Markov CCE in two-player general-sum stochastic games via turn-based constructions in which each state is controlled by a single player, with control alternating across states. This structure forces every Markov CCE to collapse to a Nash equilibrium (NE), so hardness for NE transfers immediately to CCE. It remained open whether hardness persists when a single player controls all transitions--a setting where no such collapse occurs. We resolve this question: computing an approximate stationary Markov CCE in two-player single-controller stochastic games is PPAD-complete, even with a fixed discount factor and binary actions. For the perfect notion (equilibrium constraints at every state) this holds unconditionally at constant accuracy; for the non-perfect notion, we prove constant-accuracy hardness under the PCP-for-PPAD hypothesis [BPR16, DFHM26] and inverse-polynomial-accuracy hardness unconditionally. To the best of our knowledge, our result is the first to show hardness for computing CCE without relying on equilibrium collapse phenomena or other routes through Nash-like structure [FGK23, AKSZ24, PR24]. Instead, we construct single-controller gadgets whose local incentive constraints force a solution

verdict.claim: The authors establish PPAD-hardness for computing approximate stationary Markov coarse correlated equilibria in two-player single-controller stochastic games.
verdict.evidence: We resolve this question: computing an approximate stationary Markov CCE in two-player single-controller stochastic games is PPAD-complete, even with a fixed discount factor and binary actions.
verdict.caveat: The paper addresses coarse correlated equilibria in stochastic Markov games rather than the polynomial-time approximation constant for Nash equilibria in static two-player bimatrix games.

signals.title: Fisher Markets with Approximately Optimal Bundles and the Need for a PCP Theorem for PPAD
signals.abstract: We study the problem of computing a competitive equilibrium with approximately optimal bundles in Fisher markets with separable piecewise-linear concave (SPLC) utility functions, meaning that every buyer receives a $(1-δ)$-optimal bundle, instead of a perfectly optimal one. We establish the first intractability result for the problem by showing that it is PPAD-hard for some constant $δ> 0$, assuming the PCP-for-PPAD conjecture. This hardness result holds even if all buyers have identical budgets (competitive equilibrium with equal incomes), linear capped utilities, and even if we also allow $\varepsilon$-approximate clearing instead of perfect clearing, for any constant $\varepsilon < 1/9$. Importantly, we show that the PCP-for-PPAD conjecture is in fact required to show hardness for constant $δ$: showing PPAD-hardness for finding such approximate market equilibria in a broad class of markets encompassing those generated by our hardness result would prove the conjecture. This is the first natural problem where the conjecture is provably required to establish hardness for it.

verdict.claim: The paper proves conditional PPAD-hardness results for approximate competitive equilibria in Fisher markets and explores the necessity of the PCP-for-PPAD conjecture, but it does not address $\epsilon$-approximate Nash equilibria in bimatrix games.
verdict.evidence: We establish the first intractability result for the problem by showing that it is PPAD-hard for some constant $\delta> 0$, assuming the PCP-for-PPAD conjecture.
verdict.caveat: The results apply to market equilibria in Fisher markets rather than Nash equilibria in two-player games.

problems.title: P vs NC — is everything efficiently parallelisable?
problems.statement: Is $\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NC}$: does every polynomial-time problem admit a polylogarithmic-depth circuit of polynomial size?
problems.why: $\mathrm{P}$-completeness is used exactly as $\mathrm{NP}$-completeness is — as evidence that a problem resists parallelisation — and like $\mathrm{NP}$-completeness, the underlying separation is unproved.

evidence.text: The circuit value problem is $\mathrm{P}$-complete under logspace reductions, as are linear programming and maximum flow, making them the canonical hard cases.
No superpolylogarithmic depth lower bound is known for any explicit problem in $\mathrm{P}$ against unbounded fan-in circuits of polynomial size.

signals.title: A Near-Optimal Parallel Algorithm for Finding Matroid Bases
signals.abstract: We settle the classic question of the parallel complexity of computing a matroid basis, as first posed in the seminal work of Karp, Upfal, and Wigderson (FOCS 1985, JCSS 1988). Our algorithm runs in $O(n^{1/3}\log^{1/3}n)$ rounds, matching the lower bound of KUW up to a $\log^{2/3}(n)$ factor.
signals.source: arXiv search: all:"parallel algorithm" AND cat:cs.CC

verdict.claim: The authors present an $O(n^{1/3}\text{log}^{1/3}n)$-round parallel algorithm for computing a matroid basis, matching the established oracle lower bound.
verdict.evidence: Our algorithm runs in $O(n^{1/3}\log^{1/3}n)$ rounds, matching the lower bound of KUW up to a $\text{log}^{2/3}(n)$ factor.
verdict.caveat: The result addresses parallel round complexity in the independence oracle model for matroid basis computation rather than general circuit complexity bounds for $\mathrm{P}$ vs $\mathrm{NC}$.

problems.title: The sensitivity conjecture
problems.statement: Nisan–Szegedy: is the block sensitivity of a Boolean function polynomially bounded by its sensitivity? Equivalently, is sensitivity polynomially related to every other standard complexity measure (degree, certificate complexity, decision tree depth)?
problems.why: Sensitivity was the one measure left outside the polynomially-equivalent family that contains degree, block sensitivity and query complexity — a single conspicuous hole in an otherwise complete picture.

evidence.text: Gotsman–Linial reduced the conjecture to a statement about induced subgraphs of the hypercube: any induced subgraph on more than half the vertices has maximum degree $\Omega(\sqrt n)$.
The reduced statement stood for twenty-seven years before it was proved.

resolution.text: A two-page proof: a signed adjacency matrix of the hypercube has eigenvalues $\pm\sqrt n$, and eigenvalue interlacing forces any induced subgraph on more than half the vertices to have maximum degree at least $\sqrt n$. With Gotsman–Linial this gives $\mathrm{bs}(f)=O(s(f)^4)$.
resolution.title: Induced subgraphs of hypercubes and a proof of the Sensitivity Conjecture

problems.title: The Kadison–Singer problem
problems.statement: Does every pure state on the algebra of bounded diagonal operators on $\ell^2$ extend uniquely to a pure state on all bounded operators? Equivalently, in the discrete form used in TCS: Weaver's $\mathrm{KS}_2$ conjecture on partitioning isotropic vectors into two well-conditioned halves.
problems.why: Its discrete form is a statement about splitting a set of vectors so that both halves keep spectral structure — exactly what spectral sparsification and the existence of Ramanujan graphs need.

evidence.text: Anderson's paving conjecture, Weaver's $\mathrm{KS}_r$ conjectures and the Bourgain–Tzafriri restricted invertibility conjecture were all shown equivalent to the original functional-analytic statement.

resolution.by: Adam Marcus, Daniel Spielman, Nikhil Srivastava
resolution.text: The method of interlacing families of polynomials, together with a barrier-function bound on the largest root of a mixed characteristic polynomial, proves Weaver's $\mathrm{KS}_2$ and so the original conjecture. The same technique gave bipartite Ramanujan graphs of every degree.
resolution.title: Interlacing Families II: Mixed Characteristic Polynomials and the Kadison-Singer Problem

problems.title: The randomized k-server conjecture
problems.statement: Is there a randomised online algorithm for the $k$-server problem that is $O(\mathrm{polylog}\,k)$-competitive on every metric space, against oblivious adversaries?
problems.why: It was the working assumption behind two decades of metric-embedding-based online algorithms — randomness was expected to buy an exponential improvement over the deterministic bound of $k$.

evidence.text: Bubeck, Cohen, Lee, Lee and Mądry gave an $O(\mathrm{polylog}(k,n))$-competitive algorithm for $n$-point metrics, which looked like a step toward the conjecture.

resolution.by: Sébastien Bubeck, Christian Coester, Yuval Rabani
resolution.text: Refuted. They construct metric spaces on which every randomised algorithm has competitive ratio $\Omega(\log^2 k)$ growing without polylogarithmic bound in the right regime, showing the conjectured polylogarithmic ratio is impossible in general.
resolution.title: The Randomized k-Server Conjecture is False!

problems.title: The Erdős discrepancy problem
problems.statement: For every $\pm1$ sequence $(x_n)$ and every constant $C$, are there $d$ and $k$ with $\left|\sum_{i=1}^{k} x_{id}\right| > C$?
problems.why: Eighty years of an elementary-sounding question about sign sequences, and the eventual proof came from analytic number theory rather than combinatorics.

evidence.text: A Polymath5 SAT-solver computation showed that discrepancy $2$ requires sequences of length at most $1160$, settling the first non-trivial case by exhaustive search.

resolution.text: Proved, using the Elliott conjecture on correlations of multiplicative functions (established in the averaged form needed) together with the Polymath5 reduction. Discrepancy is unbounded for every $\pm1$ sequence.
resolution.title: The Erdos discrepancy problem

problems.title: The exact complexity of the art gallery problem
problems.statement: Given a simple polygon and an integer $k$, decide whether $k$ guards suffice to see the whole interior. The problem was known to be $\mathrm{NP}$-hard, but not known to be in $\mathrm{NP}$ — where exactly does it sit?
problems.why: It was the flagship example of a natural geometric problem whose membership in $\mathrm{NP}$ was in doubt, because optimal guard positions can require irrational coordinates.

evidence.text: Abrahamsen, Adamaszek and Miltzow exhibited polygons whose optimal guard placements require irrational coordinates, ruling out the obvious combinatorial certificate.

resolution.by: Mikkel Abrahamsen, Anna Adamaszek, Tillmann Miltzow
resolution.text: The problem is $\exists\mathbb{R}$-complete: it is polynomial-time equivalent to deciding the truth of an existential sentence over the reals. This places it precisely, between $\mathrm{NP}$ and $\mathrm{PSPACE}$, and explains why no $\mathrm{NP}$ membership proof was found.
resolution.title: The Art Gallery Problem is $\exists \mathbb{R}$-complete

problems.title: The Erdős distinct distances problem
problems.statement: What is the minimum number of distinct distances determined by $n$ points in the plane? Erdős conjectured $\Theta(n/\sqrt{\log n})$, achieved by the square grid.
problems.why: It was the archetype of a problem where the extremal example was obvious and the matching lower bound was not, and its resolution introduced the polynomial method to discrete geometry.

evidence.text: The $\sqrt n\times\sqrt n$ integer grid determines $\Theta(n/\sqrt{\log n})$ distinct distances, giving the conjectured upper bound immediately.
A long sequence of lower bounds crept from $n^{1/2}$ up to about $n^{0.8641}$ (Katz–Tardos) using incidence geometry.

resolution.text: Proved a lower bound of $\Omega(n/\log n)$ — matching the grid up to a $\sqrt{\log n}$ factor — via the polynomial partitioning method and an Elekes–Sharir reduction to line incidences in $\mathbb{R}^3$. The remaining logarithmic factor is still open.
resolution.title: On the Erdos distinct distance problem in the plane
